slides.title: Get started
slides.html:
Start the class 'axiom wall': postulates go on the bottom row. Every new theorem gets a card with arrows to its parents. The four 'famous theorems' preview (Jacobs 2.6) go on a separate 'not proved yet' strip.

  • I can tell the difference between postulates, definitions, and theorems.
  • I can label statements as undefined term, definition, postulate or theorem.
  • I can trace a theorem back to the statements it depends on.

slides.title: The big idea
slides.html: A deductive system specifies starting terms, definitions, postulates and rules of inference. Postulates are assumed; theorems are results proved from these ingredients without circular reasoning. Famous results not yet proved stay on the not-proved-yet strip. (In plain words: rules of inference are the allowed moves, like substituting a value or using an if-then rule. Theorems are what we build with them, not one of the starting parts.)

slides.title: Words to know
slides.html:
• deductive system A body of math built from starting terms and rules using only logic.
  • undefined (starting) term A basic word we describe but do not define.
  • definition An exact meaning built from words we already have.
  • postulate A starting rule we accept without proof.
  • rule of inference An allowed logical step from statements we have to a new one.
  • theorem A statement proved inside the system.
  • conjecture A guess that has not been proved yet.
  • not proved yet We do not know whether it is true or false, so we cannot use it as a reason.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.html:
Sort the parts of a made-up rule.

Read the worked steps
StepReason
A made-up rule says the output is z = 2x + 1.This is a definition: it tells what the rule means.
We are told x = 4.This is a given.
Then z = 2 · 4 + 1 = 9.Substitute into the rule.
The 9 is a result we figured out, not something we assumed.It comes from the rule and the given.
Second check: (9 - 1)/2 = 4, which takes us back to the input.Run the rule backward.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.html:
Check a made-up system with three points.

Read the worked steps
StepReason
Points: P, Q, R. Lines: {P, Q}, {Q, R}, {P, R}.This made-up system is the whole world for now.
Rule to check: every two different points lie on exactly one line.The axiom.
PQ is only in {P, Q}. QR is only in {Q, R}. PR is only in {P, R}.Check every pair.
So the rule holds in this little system.All three pairs pass.
But that does not make it full Euclidean geometry. Its lines have only two points, and our course's lines have infinitely many.It obeys one rule, not all of them.

slides.title: Common mistake
slides.html:
Ava says 'postulates and theorems are the same thing: both are true statements.'

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Find and fix the error

A postulate is assumed without proof. A theorem must be proved from postulates and definitions. Sort the cards into three categories: ASSUMED, DEFINED and PROVED. "Everything in U is in V" is assumed. "W means in both U and V" is defined. "U=W" follows by proving both containments, so it is proved: a theorem, not another postulate.

geo.title: Common mistake
geo.prompt: Ava says 'postulates and theorems are the same thing: both are true statements.'
geo.correction: A postulate is assumed without proof. A theorem must be proved from postulates and definitions. Sort the cards into three categories: ASSUMED, DEFINED and PROVED. "Everything in U is in V" is assumed. "W means in both U and V" is defined. "U=W" follows by proving both containments, so it is proved: a theorem, not another postulate.

slides.title: Practice 1
slides.html:
A system assumes: everything in group U is also in group V. It defines W as 'in both U and V.' Prove that U and W have exactly the same members.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

If something is in U, the rule puts it in V too, so it is in both: it is in W. If something is in W, it is in U by the definition. Each group holds the other, so U = W.

Reveal second check

W is the overlap of U and V. When U sits inside V, the overlap is all of U.

slides.title: Practice 2
slides.html:
Theorem T is proved using lemma L. The only proof of L uses T. Neither one is a postulate. Has either been proved?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

No. They lean on each other in a circle, and nothing connects them to the postulates. Fix: prove one of them another way, or openly add one as a postulate.

Reveal second check

The arrows T to L to T make a loop. A loop never starts at the postulates, no matter how believable T and L are.

slides.title: Practice 3
slides.html:
A conjecture has been measured carefully in 300 drawings. The author lists it as a theorem with no proof. What are the two honest choices?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Keep calling it a conjecture, or openly add it as a new postulate and say the system has changed. Measurements don't make it a theorem.

Reveal second check

'Theorem' means it was proved from the current postulates. More drawings or a new label can't supply that proof.

slides.html:
Where does 'a triangle's angles add up to a straight angle' go on the axiom wall today?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

On the 'not proved yet' strip. We will prove it later in the course.
